messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Using git bisect
parts:
Hi everyone -

I've recently become a fan of using git bisect to find the sources of bugs.

Briefly, if you know that the current commit is bad, and that some previous commit is good, then you can use git bisect to find the commit that introduced the bug, using a binary search. It checks out a commit somewhere in the middle if the known good and bad commits, then you test and tell it whether the commit is good or bad; this process is repeated until you find the first bad commit. This usually makes it a lot easier to find the cause.

Testing can be automated if you write a script to run the tests. You can just start the testing and walk away, and a couple minutes later, it will report the commit that introduced the bug. 

I've written up how to use git bisect with ggplot2 here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Using-git-bisect-to-hunt-bugs
The page also includes some example scripts for automatic testing, which should be easy to customize.

Feedback is welcomed!
-Winston

On Wed, Feb 1, 2012 at 9:08 AM, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> Well, I'm not so sure -- sometimes the problem you're trying to fix is that
> the code is throws an error when run (the first example has this problem).
> In these cases, if pass/fail were represented by a TRUE/FALSE return value,
> the test code would still have to be wrapped in a tryCatch(), which would
> catch the error and return FALSE.
>
> Still, I think it should be possible to simplify telling it what to do when
> an error is thrown.

True - the bisect function could have an on_error parameter = c(F, T, NA).

Hadley


In addition to values for return good/bad/skip, I think there also has to be one for "do nothing and keep running the R script".

For example, in one of the tests I wrote, there are two stages:
1. Load the library with load_all(). If this throws an error, quit and return SKIP. Otherwise, continue running the script.
2. Run the actual test. If it runs, quit and return GOOD; if it throws an error, quit and return BAD.


-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Using git bisect
parts:
I was thinking that this would be taken care of at the devtools level
- i.e. it would load the package for you, and skip if it errors on
load.

OK, I have something that works and gives a reasonably clean interface. Here's an example of a fully-automated test script:

#/usr/bin/Rscript
cat("\n===== Running test script ======\n")
library(devtools)

# If error loading, skip this commit
bisect_load_all('.', on_error = NA)

# The test code
testRun <- function() {
  dat <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=1:3)
  
  # Bad: Throws error when breaks=NA
  p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks=NA)    
  x11()
  print(p)
  
  # If it reaches this point, then it successfully printed. Mark GOOD
  return(TRUE)
}

# Run the test. If error, mark BAD
bisect_test(testRun, on_error = FALSE)

 

And here's an example of a test function that requires interactive response (for brevity, I won't repeat the loading code at top):

# A test that requires visual inspection and manual response
testRunInteractive <- function() {
  dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:5], y=1, z=(1:5)/4)
  
  # Bad: Show's NA at high and low end of legend
  p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=z)) + geom_bar()

  # Need to manually open x11 window because we're in a script
  x11()
  print(p)

  # User must visually inspect and mark good/bad/skip
  bisect_return_interactive()
}

# Run the test. If error, mark SKIP
bisect_test(testRunInteractive, on_error = NA)


I've put the function definitions here -- this is the stuff that would go in devtools:
https://gist.github.com/1721649


In addition to TRUE=good, FALSE=bad, and NA=skip, I added NULL=do nothing (continue running script). I made use it when running load_all(), which returns NULL. It will also be useful if someone wants to run a two-stage test like this:
1. Setup stuff (after the load_all) - if error here, SKIP
2. The actual test - if error here, BAD

setupStuff <- function() {
  # Do some setup stuff
  return(NULL)
}
bisect_test(setupStuff, on_error = NA)
bisect_test(realTest, on_error = FALSE)

It's conceivable that there would be breakage in the setup part -- that something else broke that prevents you from getting to the important part of the test. (I've seen some really ... interesting stuff when jumping around the commit history with a bisect. Things work pretty well at the beginning (0.8.9) and at the end (0.9.0), but in the middle it gets pretty weird.)

Let me know what you think of this version (structure, function names, etc)... If it looks good, I'll add it to a branch on devtools.
-Winston
